children.title: MIR Closure
children.top_down_role: Closure structures generated by mixed-integer rounding cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: MIR Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation-relative closure generated by all one-row mixed-integer rounding cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a rational mixed-integer formulation \(P(A,b,I)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b,\ x_i\in\mathbb Z\text{ for }i\in I\}\), together with its variable bounds. Let \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{MIR}}(A,b,I)\) denote all inequalities obtained by taking a nonnegative aggregation of rows of \(Ax\le b\), substituting valid bounds, and applying the one-row mixed-integer rounding rule. The MIR closure of this formulation is
\[
\operatorname{MIR}(A,b,I)=\{x\in\operatorname{LP}(A,b):\alpha^Tx\le\beta\text{ for every }(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal R_{\mathrm{MIR}}(A,b,I)\}.
\]
Because the generating rows and bounds belong to the formulation, equivalent or extended formulations can yield different MIR closures in the original variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The MIR closure enforces every mixed-integer rounding inequality obtainable from aggregated rows and bounds of a fixed formulation, so it can depend on that formulation.
assumptions_latex: The formulation includes the bounds used by MIR rounding.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{MIR}(A,b,I)\) is the intersection of the LP relaxation with all formulation-generated MIR halfspaces.

notation.meaning: continuous relaxation of the fixed formulation
family of inequalities generated by one-row MIR rounding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The formulation-relative MIR family is described informally, and neither the exact generating operator nor the claimed representation dependence has a cited source. Those choices materially affect the closure being defined.

children.title: GMI Closure
children.top_down_role: Closure structures generated by Gomory mixed-integer cuts.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation is a rational polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\) with designated integer coordinates \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
A fixed linear or tableau representation \(R\) of \(P\) is used to generate GMI inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_I\subseteq \operatorname{GMI}(P;R)\subseteq P.\]

notation.meaning: Mixed-integer hull of the represented relaxation.
Family of all GMI inequalities generated from eligible rows of the fixed representation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the representation-specific, one-round GMI closure of a rational mixed-integer relaxation.

source_refs.locator: 9.4 Using Lift-and-Project to Choose the Best Mixed Integer Gomory Cut p. 117

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each inequality \(\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) in the family \(\mathcal{G}(R)\) obtained by applying the Gomory mixed-integer construction to an eligible row of \(R\), define the GMI closure by
\[\operatorname{GMI}(P;R):=P\cap\bigcap_{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal{G}(R)}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\alpha^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\}.\]
Every member of \(\mathcal{G}(R)\) is valid for \(P_I\); hence the closure retains the mixed-integer hull and can only strengthen the original relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The GMI closure intersects a fixed relaxation with every GMI inequality generated from its chosen representation; it contains the mixed-integer hull and is contained in the relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: GMI Closure

children.top_down_role: Closure relationships that vary with row or tableau representation.

assumptions_latex: Two representations \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) describe relaxations whose mixed-integer feasible points have the same projection \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).

notation.meaning: Two formulations or tableau representations of the same projected mixed-integer set.
Projection from formulation space to the common original-variable space.
GMI closure generated in representation space.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes validity, which is formulation invariant, from one-round closure strength, which need not be.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: GMI generation is an operation on rows of a chosen formulation, not solely on its projected mixed-integer set. Consequently, both projected closures \(\pi_1(\operatorname{GMI}(R_1))\) and \(\pi_2(\operatorname{GMI}(R_2))\) contain \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\), but they need not coincide. Adding variables, constraints, or alternative tableau rows can change the available one-row MIR-GMI inequalities. Thus a row-wise MIR-GMI correspondence does not imply that arbitrary formulations of the same set have identical one-round MIR or GMI closures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: GMI cuts are row- and formulation-dependent. Equivalent mixed-integer formulations retain the same integer hull but can yield different projected one-round GMI closures.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Facet bounds for elementary disjunctive hulls and the lift-and-project closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded quantitative bound using the source's notation for the elementary lift-and-project construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(k\in\{1,\ldots,p\}\), the polyhedron \(\operatorname{conv}(P_{k0}\cup P_{k1})\) has at most \(\binom{m+p+n-1}{n}\) facets. Consequently, the elementary closure \(\bigcap_{k=1}^{p}P_k\) of \(P\) with respect to the lift-and-project operation has at most \(p\binom{m+p+n-1}{n}\) facets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each elementary disjunctive hull has at most binomial(m+p+n−1,n) facets. Consequently, the intersection of the p associated lift-and-project polyhedra has at most p times that number of facets.
assumptions_latex: \(P_{k0},P_{k1},P_k\) and \(m,p,n\) have the meanings assigned in the elementary lift-and-project construction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\!\left(\operatorname{conv}(P_{k0}\cup P_{k1})\right)\leq \binom{m+p+n-1}{n},\qquad f\!\left(\bigcap_{k=1}^{p}P_k\right)\leq p\binom{m+p+n-1}{n}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixed-binary lift-and-project inequalities and closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-binary-variable disjunctive convexifications of a mixed 0–1 polyhedral relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\subseteq\{x:0\le x_j\le1\ (j\in I)\}\), and let \(S=P\cap\{x:x_j\in\{0,1\}\ (j\in I)\}\). For \(j\in I\), define \(P_j=\operatorname{conv}((P\cap\{x:x_j=0\})\cup(P\cap\{x:x_j=1\}))\). An inequality \(\alpha^\top x\le\beta\) is a lift-and-project inequality if and only if it is valid for \(P_j\) for some \(j\in I\). The lift-and-project closure is \(P^{\mathrm{lift}}=\bigcap_{j\in I}P_j\). Every \(P_j\), and hence \(P^{\mathrm{lift}}\), is polyhedral, and \(P^{\mathrm{split}}\subseteq P^{\mathrm{lift}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each designated binary variable, convexify the two faces obtained by fixing it to zero and one. Lift-and-project inequalities are exactly those valid for one of these convexifications, and the lift-and-project closure is their intersection over all designated variables. The closure is polyhedral and contains the split closure.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\subseteq\{x\in\mathbb R^n:0\le x_j\le1\ \forall j\in I\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P^{\mathrm{lift}}=\bigcap_{j\in I}P_j\text{ is a polyhedron and }P^{\mathrm{split}}\subseteq P^{\mathrm{lift}}.

children.title: Disjunctive Closures
children.top_down_role: Closures produced through disjunctive convexification.

assumptions_latex: The indexed disjunctions \(D^k=\bigcup_{t=1}^{q_k}\{x:(d^{kt})^{\mathsf T}x\le\delta_{kt}\}\) are valid for the intended discrete feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_I\subseteq \mathcal{D}(P)\subseteq P.\]

notation.meaning: Convexified portion of the relaxation satisfying disjunction k.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a one-round closure for a specified family of finite valid disjunctions.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Valid Inequalities for Disjunctive Sets p. 9

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each valid disjunction \(D^k\), its disjunctive relaxation is \(P^{D^k}:=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap D^k)\). The disjunctive closure associated with the family \(\{D^k:k\in K\}\) is
\[\mathcal{D}(P):=\bigcap_{k\in K}P^{D^k}.\]
Equivalently, it is the intersection of \(P\) with all linear inequalities valid for every set \(P\cap D^k\), for every \(k\in K\). Since each disjunction contains every intended discrete feasible point, \(P_I\subseteq\mathcal{D}(P)\), while convexification and intersection give \(\mathcal{D}(P)\subseteq P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disjunctive closure intersects the convex hulls obtained by imposing each valid disjunction on the relaxation, retaining the discrete hull while strengthening the relaxation.

children.title: Lift–Project Closures
children.top_down_role: Closures produced through lift–project operators.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation is a polyhedron \(P\subseteq[0,1]^p\times\mathbb{R}^{n-p}\), and the coordinates indexed by \(J:=\{1,\ldots,p\}\) are designated binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_I\subseteq \operatorname{LP}(P)\subseteq P.\]

notation.meaning: Binary disjunction associated with coordinate j.
Original-space elementary lift-and-project set for coordinate j.
Convex hull of the binary feasible points of P.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Lift-and-Project Cuts for Mixed 0-1 Programs p. 79

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each \(j\in J\), define the original-space elementary lift-and-project set by
\[L_j(P):=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((P\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x_j=0\})\cup(P\cap\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x_j=1\})\bigr).\]
Equivalently, \(L_j(P)\) is the projection onto the original variables of the standard lifted formulation for the binary disjunction \(D_j\). The one-round elementary lift-and-project closure is
\[\operatorname{LP}(P):=\bigcap_{j\in J}L_j(P).\]
It satisfies \(P_I\subseteq\operatorname{LP}(P)\subseteq P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each designated binary coordinate, the elementary lift-and-project set is the convex hull of the two parts obtained by fixing that coordinate to zero or one. The one-round closure intersects these sets over all designated binary coordinates and lies between the binary feasible hull and the original relaxation.

children.title: Closure Containment Relations
children.top_down_role: Containment and equivalence regimes across the two closure families.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation is a polyhedron \(P\subseteq[0,1]^p\times\mathbb{R}^{n-p}\), with binary-designated index set \(J:=\{1,\ldots,p\}\).
The family \(\mathfrak{F}\) consists of valid disjunctions for the binary feasible points and contains every elementary binary disjunction \(D_j:=\{x:x_j=0\}\cup\{x:x_j=1\}\), \(j\in J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P_I\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{F}}(P)\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{01}(P)=\operatorname{LP}(P)\subseteq P.\]

notation.meaning: Closure obtained from every disjunction in the specified family F.
Intersection of the elementary binary disjunctive hulls.
Elementary binary lift-and-project closure in the original-variable space.
Convex hull of the binary feasible points of P.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(j\in J\), the original-space projection of the elementary lift-and-project formulation equals the corresponding binary disjunctive hull:
\[L_j(P)=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap D_j).\]
Consequently, the matching one-round closures satisfy
\[\operatorname{LP}(P)=\mathcal{D}_{01}(P).\]
Because \(\mathfrak{F}\) contains all the disjunctions \(D_j\), the associated closures obey
\[P_I\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\mathfrak{F}}(P)\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{01}(P)=\operatorname{LP}(P)\subseteq P.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The elementary binary lift-and-project closure equals the closure formed from the matching binary disjunctions. A specified valid-disjunction family containing all those binary disjunctions produces a closure contained in that common closure, while still containing the binary feasible hull.

children.title: Chvátal–Gomory Rank
children.top_down_role: Inequality, polyhedral, and reverse-rank regimes for Chvátal–Gomory closure.

assumptions_latex: The initial relaxation is a rational polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[r_{\mathrm{CG}}(P)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}:P^{(t)}=P_I\}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}\cup\{\infty\}.\]

notation.meaning: Iterated CG closure, initialized by the original relaxation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines polyhedral CG rank; inequality rank is obtained by first-round validity under the same iteration.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.2 The Cutting Plane Method p. 11

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(P^{(0)}:=P\) and recursively define \(P^{(t+1)}:=\operatorname{CG}(P^{(t)})\), where \(\operatorname{CG}(Q)\) is the intersection of all Chvátal-Gomory inequalities for \(Q\). The Chvátal-Gomory rank of \(P\) is
\[r_{\mathrm{CG}}(P):=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}:P^{(t)}=P_I\},\]
with value \(\infty\) if no such \(t\) exists. For an inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le b\) valid for \(P_I\), its CG rank relative to \(P\) is the least \(t\) for which it is valid on \(P^{(t)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CG rank is the least number of iterated Chvátal-Gomory closure rounds needed to reach the integer hull; an inequality's rank is its first valid round.

children.top_down_role: Finite, unbounded, and infinite split-rank regimes.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation is a polyhedron \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) with integer-designated coordinates indexed by \(I\).
The split closure uses all splits \(\pi^{\mathsf T}x_I\le\pi_0\) or \(\pi^{\mathsf T}x_I\ge\pi_0+1\), where \(\pi\in\mathbb{Z}^{I}\) and \(\pi_0\in\mathbb{Z}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P^{[0]}:=P\) and \(P^{[t+1]}:=\operatorname{SC}(P^{[t]})\), where \(\operatorname{SC}(Q)\) intersects the convexified disjunctive relaxations of \(Q\) over all integer splits. The split rank of \(P\) is
\[r_{\mathrm{split}}(P):=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}:P^{[t]}=P_I\}.\]
The rank is finite when this equality holds after finitely many rounds and is \(\infty\) otherwise. The split rank of an inequality valid for \(P_I\) is the least \(t\) at which it is valid for \(P^{[t]}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split rank counts repeated all-splits closure rounds until the mixed-integer hull is reached; failure at every finite round gives infinite rank.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[r_{\mathcal{D}}(P):=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}:P^{t}=P_I\},\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Disjunctive rank under sequential convexification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the disjunctive rank of a valid inequality for a sequentially convexifiable mixed 0–1 system, gives the binary-variable upper bound, and records its failure as a universal Chvátal-rank bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) have \(p\) designated binary variables and let \(\pi\) be an ordering of \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\). Set \(P_0=P\) and \(P_j=\operatorname{conv}\{x\in P_{j-1}:x_{\pi(j)}\in\{0,1\}\}\) for \(j=1,\ldots,p\). The disjunctive rank of \(\alpha^\top x\ge\beta\) is the smallest \(k\) for which there exists an ordering \(\pi\) such that the inequality is valid for \(P_k\). Thus it can be obtained in \(k\), but not fewer than \(k\), recursive convexification steps. For a valid cutting plane in a sequentially convexifiable mixed \(0\)-\(1\) system, this rank is at most \(p\). The number \(p\) is not, in general, an upper bound for the Chv\'atal rank of an inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After ordering the binary variables, impose one binary restriction and convexify at each stage. An inequality's disjunctive rank is the fewest stages, over all orderings, needed to make it valid. For a valid cutting plane in a sequentially convexifiable mixed 0–1 system, the rank is at most the number of binary variables; that number does not universally bound Chvátal rank.
assumptions_latex: \alpha^\top x\ge\beta\text{ is a valid cutting plane for the mixed }0\text{--}1\text{ set when applying the upper bound}
\text{The mixed }0\text{--}1\text{ system is sequentially convexifiable when applying the upper bound}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{rank}_{D}(\alpha^\top x\ge\beta)=\min\{k:\exists\pi\text{ such that }\alpha^\top x\ge\beta\text{ is valid for }P_k\},\qquad \operatorname{rank}_{D}\le p,\quad\text{but }p\text{ is not a universal upper bound on Chv\'atal rank.}

children.title: Rank Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings where the two rank notions coincide or diverge.

assumptions_latex: The initial relaxation is a polyhedron \(P\subseteq[0,1]^p\times\mathbb{R}^{n-p}\), and \(P_I:=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap(\{0,1\}^p\times\mathbb{R}^{n-p}))\).
The disjunctive closure operator \(\mathcal{D}\) and lift-and-project closure operator \(\mathcal{L}\) act in the same original-variable space and use matching elementary binary disjunctions.
For every relaxation \(Q\) in the common iteration orbit of \(P\), \(\mathcal{L}(Q)=\mathcal{D}(Q)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal{L}^{t}(P)=\mathcal{D}^{t}(P)\quad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0},\qquad r_{\mathcal{L}}(P)=r_{\mathcal{D}}(P).\]

notation.meaning: Matching disjunctive and lift-and-project closure operators.
Their t-fold iterates, with zeroth iterate equal to the identity.
Ranks relative to the two operators and the common target hull.
Convex hull of the binary feasible points of P.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank equality is asserted only for operators that coincide throughout the full iteration orbit in the same projected space.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 8. The Correspondence Between Lift-and-Project Cuts and Simple Disjunctive Cuts p. 97
6.1 Disjunctive Rank p. 80

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal{D}^{0}(P)=\mathcal{L}^{0}(P):=P\), and define subsequent iterates by composition. Under the stated operator-equality assumption,
\[\mathcal{L}^{t}(P)=\mathcal{D}^{t}(P)\quad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}.\]
Define
\[r_{\mathcal{L}}(P):=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}:\mathcal{L}^{t}(P)=P_I\},\qquad r_{\mathcal{D}}(P):=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}:\mathcal{D}^{t}(P)=P_I\}.\]
Then
\[r_{\mathcal{L}}(P)=r_{\mathcal{D}}(P),\]
including when the common value is \(\infty\). The same equality of first-valid rounds holds for every inequality valid for \(P_I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the matching lift-and-project and disjunctive operators coincide on every relaxation reached during iteration, all of their iterates coincide. Their polyhedral ranks and the first-valid rounds of valid inequalities are therefore equal, including the infinite-rank case.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the classical pure-integer Gomory cutting-plane procedure. At iteration \(t\), if the lexicographically selected optimal basic solution \(x^{t}\) is nonintegral, generate a Gomory fractional cut from the prescribed nonintegral basic row, append it, and restore optimality by the prescribed lexicographic dual-simplex rule. Under the stated feasibility, boundedness, rationality, and selection assumptions, the lexicographic tableau measure improves strictly after each nonterminal iteration. Hence the procedure performs only finitely many cut-and-reoptimization steps and terminates at an optimal integer solution.

children.title: Gomory Convergence Failure Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Gomory Convergence Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the classical finite-termination guarantee, not a claim that every unprotected execution fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a Gomory cutting-plane execution for a rational pure-integer linear program. Classical finite-convergence reasoning depends on exact arithmetic, a prescribed lexicographic or otherwise well-founded selection rule, and cuts satisfying the required integrality construction. If these safeguards are removed, finite termination is no longer implied: arbitrary pivot or cut choices may revisit equivalent bases, while an infinite sequence of improving relaxations may approach the integer optimum without attaining it finitely. The same proof does not automatically extend to irrational data or unrestricted mixed-integer tableaux, because its discrete well-founded measure can be absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without exact arithmetic, valid Gomory cuts, and a well-founded selection rule, the classical proof gives no finite-termination guarantee; cycling or asymptotic progress may occur.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation is solved repeatedly after adding Gomory-type cuts
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Finite convergence cannot be inferred once the classical discrete-progress safeguards are absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Mixed-Binary Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard bounded polyhedral setting for finite lift-and-project convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-binary relaxation is in the bounded regime when \(P=\{(x,y)\in[0,1]^p\times\mathbb{R}^q:A x+B y\le d\}\) is a nonempty bounded rational polyhedron and the intended feasible set is \(F=P\cap(\{0,1\}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q)\). Every branch \(P\cap\{x_i=0\}\) and \(P\cap\{x_i=1\}\) is then compact, so its convex hull and every finite disjunctive convexification are closed polyhedra. This regime supplies the compactness needed by the usual finite-depth lift-and-project hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime consists of bounded rational relaxations with finitely many binary variables; all binary branches and finite disjunctive convexifications are closed polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Lift–Project Closure Depth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-rank statement for the standard bounded mixed-binary lift-and-project hierarchy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq[0,1]^p\times\mathbb{R}^q\) be a bounded rational polyhedron, and define \(P^0=P\). For a relaxation \(Q\), let \(L(Q)\) denote the standard lift-and-project closure obtained by imposing every elementary disjunction \(x_i=0\ \vee\ x_i=1\), \(i=1,\ldots,p\), in its lifted formulation and projecting back. Then the hierarchy has rank at most \(p\): \[P^p=\operatorname{conv}\bigl(P\cap(\{0,1\}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q)\bigr).\] Consequently, no more than \(p\) closure rounds are required for exact mixed-binary convexification.

children.title: Unbounded-Regime Limitations

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Regime Limitations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonclosed disjunctive hulls explain why bounded finite-depth statements need recession qualifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Boundedness cannot simply be deleted from a closed-convexification argument. Let \(D_0=\{(0,0)\}\) and \(D_1=\{(1,t):t\ge1\}\). Both disjuncts are closed polyhedra, but \(\operatorname{conv}(D_0\cup D_1)\) is not closed: \((1/k,1)\) belongs to it for every integer \(k\ge1\), whereas its limit \((0,1)\) does not. Thus replacing convex hulls by closed convex hulls can add recession-limit points. In unbounded mixed-binary systems, finite lift-and-project convergence therefore requires compatible recession cones or another hypothesis ensuring closedness and exact projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unbounded disjuncts can have a nonclosed convex hull, so closed lift-and-project operations may add limit points unless recession behavior is controlled.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}(D_0\cup D_1)\) is not closed, so bounded-regime convergence arguments do not transfer without recession conditions.

children.title: Sequential Convexification Conditions

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Convexification Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stagewise condition for convexifying a finite sequence of binary disjunctions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq[0,1]^p\times\mathbb{R}^q\), fix an ordering \(i_1,
\ldots,i_p\), and set \(Q_0=P\). The system is sequentially convexifiable in this ordering if, for every \(k=1,\ldots,p\), the hull \[Q_k=\operatorname{conv}\bigl((Q_{k-1}\cap\{x_{i_k}=0\})\cup(Q_{k-1}\cap\{x_{i_k}=1\})\bigr)\] is closed and equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{z\in P:x_{i_1},\ldots,x_{i_k}\in\{0,1\}\}\). Under these stagewise facial and closedness conditions, \(Q_p=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap(\{0,1\}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential convexification is exact when every binary disjunction produces the closed hull of points satisfying all integrality conditions imposed so far.
assumptions_latex: An ordering \(i_1,\ldots,i_p\) of the binary coordinates is fixed
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated stagewise equalities imply \(Q_p=\operatorname{conv}(P\cap(\{0,1\}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q))\).

knowledge_statements.title: Chvátal–Gomory Closure Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-one Chvátal–Gomory closure for a rational pure-integer relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb{Q}^m\), and \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax\le b\}\). For every \(u\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\) satisfying \(u^{\mathsf T}A\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), the associated Chvátal–Gomory inequality is \((u^{\mathsf T}A)x\le\lfloor u^{\mathsf T}b\rfloor\). The rank-one Chvátal–Gomory closure is \[P_{\mathrm{CG}}=P\cap\bigcap_{\substack{u\in\mathbb{R}_+^m\\u^{\mathsf T}A\in\mathbb{Z}^n}}\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:(u^{\mathsf T}A)x\le\lfloor u^{\mathsf T}b\rfloor\}.\] It satisfies \(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\subseteq P_{\mathrm{CG}}\subseteq P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Chvátal–Gomory closure intersects a rational pure-integer relaxation with every inequality obtained by nonnegative aggregation followed by rounding when the aggregated left-hand side is integral.
assumptions_latex: All \(n\) coordinates of the target points are integer-restricted
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\cap\mathbb{Z}^n\subseteq P_{\mathrm{CG}}\subseteq P\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure inclusion when every variable is integer-restricted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:A x\le b\}\) be rational and regard every coordinate as integer-restricted. Each Chvátal–Gomory inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\lfloor\beta\rfloor\), obtained from a valid inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\beta\) with \(a\in\mathbb{Z}^n\), is enforced by the split disjunction \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\lfloor\beta\rfloor\ \vee\ a^{\mathsf T}x\ge\lfloor\beta\rfloor+1\), whose second branch is empty in \(P\). Hence \[P_{\mathrm{split}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{CG}}.\] Thus the split closure is at least as strong as the rank-one Chvátal–Gomory closure under the pure-integer convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For pure-integer rational polyhedra, every Chvátal–Gomory cut is captured by a split disjunction, so the split closure is at least as strong.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{\mathrm{split}}\subseteq P_{\mathrm{CG}}\).
review_flags: A theorem-level source locator is needed for the pure-integer closure inclusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The pure-integer inclusion is plausible and precisely stated, but it has no citation and includes proof-style derivation. A sourced statement without the derivation is required.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Comparison Regimes
children.top_down_role: Relative closure strength in mixed-integer settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Comparison Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison using mixed-integer CG cuts whose continuous coefficients vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\) be rational, with \(x\in\mathbb{Z}^p\) and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^q\). Define the mixed-integer Chvátal–Gomory closure using aggregated valid inequalities \(a^{\mathsf T}x+0^{\mathsf T}y\leeta\) with \(a\in\mathbb{Z}^p\), rounded to \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\lflooreta\rfloor\). Every such cut is induced by the split \(a^{\mathsf T}x\le\lflooreta\rfloor\ \\vee\ a^{\mathsf T}x\ge\lflooreta\rfloor+1\). Therefore \[P_{\mathrm{split}}
\subseteq P_{\mathrm{MICG}}.\] The comparison depends on this zero-continuous-coefficient convention; unrestricted rounding of continuous coefficients is not valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standard mixed-integer CG convention, split closure dominates the CG closure; continuous-variable coefficients cannot be rounded as integer coefficients.
assumptions_latex: Mixed-integer CG aggregation has zero coefficients on \(y\) before rounding
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(P_{\mathrm{split}}
\subseteq P_{\mathrm{MICG}}\).

notation.meaning: mixed-integer Chvátal–Gomory closure under the stated convention

review_flags: Mixed-integer CG terminology varies; a source must confirm the selected convention and inclusion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mixed-integer CG convention and resulting inclusion require an authoritative source because terminology varies. The strings \leeta and \lflooreta are malformed and must be repaired after the convention is sourced.

children.title: Split-Cut Representation
children.top_down_role: Split-cut representations relevant to equivalence results.

knowledge_statements.title: Split-Cut Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disjunctive-hull representation of a cut generated by one split.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p+q}\), write each point as \((x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^p\times\mathbb{R}^q\), and designate \(x\) as integer-restricted. Fix \(\pi\in\mathbb{Z}^p\) and \(k\in\mathbb{Z}\), and define \[D=(P\cap\{(x,y):\pi^{\mathsf T}x\le k\})\cup(P\cap\{(x,y):\pi^{\mathsf T}x\ge k+1\}).\] For \(a\in\mathbb{R}^p\), \(c\in\mathbb{R}^q\), and \(\eta\in\mathbb{R}\), the inequality \(a^{\mathsf T}x+c^{\mathsf T}y\le\eta\) is a split cut for this disjunction exactly when it is valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\). Any point of \(P\) that it removes lies in the open slab \(k<\pi^{\mathsf T}x<k+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A split cut is precisely an inequality valid for the convex hull of the two sides of an integer split disjunction.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\mathbb{R}^p\) denotes the integer-restricted coordinates and \(y\in\mathbb{R}^q\) the continuous coordinates
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The split cuts for \((\pi,k)\) are exactly the linear inequalities valid for \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\).

notation.meaning: union of the two split branches
normal and offset of the split disjunction
coefficients and right-hand side of a candidate split cut

children.title: MIR Representation
children.top_down_role: Mixed-integer rounding representations relevant to equivalence results.

knowledge_statements.title: MIR Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-row mixed-integer rounding representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Z}\), write \(b=\lfloor b\rfloor+f\) with \(0<f<1\), and define \[S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{R}_+:x+y\ge b\}.\] The elementary mixed-integer rounding inequality for this representation is \[x+\frac{y}{f}\ge\lceil b\rceil.\] Equivalently, it is \(fx+y\ge f\lceil b\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integer x, nonnegative continuous y, and nonintegral b, the constraint x plus y at least b admits the MIR inequality x plus y divided by the fractional part of b at least the ceiling of b.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x+\frac{y}{f}\ge\lceil b\rceil\).

source_refs.locator: 9.4 Using Lift-and-Project to Choose the Best Mixed Integer Gomory Cut p. 117

children.title: GMI Representation
children.top_down_role: Tableau-based GMI representations relevant to equivalence results.

knowledge_statements.title: GMI Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tableau-row form of the Gomory mixed-integer inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the tableau row \(x_B=b-\sum_{j\in I\cup C}a_jx_j\), where \(x_B\) and every \(x_j\) with \(j\in I\) are integer, every nonbasic variable is nonnegative, and \(f_0=b-\lfloor b\rfloor\in(0,1)\). For each \(j\in I\), define \(f_j=a_j-\lfloor a_j\rfloor\). The GMI inequality is \[\sum_{j\in I}\min\left\{\frac{f_j}{f_0},\frac{1-f_j}{1-f_0}\right\}x_j+\sum_{j\in C}\max\left\{\frac{a_j}{f_0},\frac{-a_j}{1-f_0}\right\}x_j\ge1.\] It is the strengthened intersection-cut representation associated with the split \(x_B\le\lfloor b\rfloor\ \vee\ x_B\ge\lceil b\rceil\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional integer tableau row yields the GMI inequality, which is the coefficient-strengthened intersection cut for the split on its basic integer variable.
assumptions_latex: \(x_B=b-\sum_{j\in I\cup C}a_jx_j\), with all nonbasic variables nonnegative
\(x_B\) and \(x_j\) for every \(j\in I\) are integer
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed inequality is valid for the tableau set and represents the strengthened split cut associated with the row.

notation.meaning: integer and continuous nonbasic index sets
fractional parts of the tableau right-hand side and integer-variable coefficients

children.title: Representation-Dependent Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Equivalence regimes determined by row, tableau, or formulation representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation-Dependent Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of split, MIR, and GMI cuts after translating between tableau, inequality, and lifted representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a rational mixed-integer relaxation, and let \(D=\{x:\pi^Tx\leq\pi_0\}\cup\{x:\pi^Tx\geq\pi_0+1\}\), where \(\pi\) is integral on the integer variables and zero on the continuous variables. A cut obtained by applying mixed-integer rounding to a valid inequality representing this split, or by applying the GMI formula to an equivalent tableau row, represents a supporting inequality of \(\operatorname{conv}(P\cap D)\). After substitution of slack variables, complementation of bounded variables, and positive rescaling, the resulting inequalities define the same halfspace. Their coefficient vectors need not coincide before these representation changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Split, MIR, and GMI cuts can define the same halfspace after tableau substitutions, variable complementation, and positive scaling, although their displayed coefficients may differ.
assumptions_latex: The compared row and inequality encode the same split disjunction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The translated MIR and GMI inequalities define the same supporting halfspace of \(\operatorname{conv}(P\cap D)\).

source_refs.locator: 9.4 Using Lift-and-Project to Choose the Best Mixed Integer Gomory Cut p. 117

source_witnesses.locator: 9.4 Using Lift-and-Project to Choose the Best Mixed Integer Gomory Cut p. 117

Moreover, validity for the disjunctive hull does not by itself imply that an inequality is supporting. An authoritative result specifying the admissible row/inequality transformations and exact equivalence hypotheses is required.

children.title: Intersection Lift-Project Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Correspondence and irregularity boundaries between geometric and lifted cuts.

children.title: Intersection-Cut Representation
children.top_down_role: Geometric representations of cuts derived from lattice-free intersections.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection-Cut Representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balas intersection cut from a conic relaxation and an open convex forbidden region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{\bar x+\sum_{j=1}^m r^js_j:s\in\mathbb R_+^m\}\), and let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex with \(\bar x\in S\) and no feasible mixed-integer point in \(S\). For each ray define \(\rho_j=\sup\{t\geq0:\bar x+tr^j\in S\}\), using \(1/\infty=0\). Every point of \(C\setminus S\), and hence every feasible mixed-integer point represented in \(C\), satisfies \[\sum_{j=1}^m \frac{s_j}{\rho_j}\geq1.\] Thus the ray-intersection distances give an explicit valid inequality in the cone variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal distances from the cone apex to a forbidden convex region's boundary are the coefficients of a valid intersection cut.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) is open, convex, contains \(\bar x\), and contains no feasible mixed-integer point.
\(C\) is represented by finitely many nonnegative rays from \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every feasible represented point satisfies \(\sum_j s_j/\rho_j\geq1\).

notation.meaning: The conic relaxation based at the cut-off point.
Exit distance of ray \(r^j\) from the forbidden region.

children.title: Lift–Project Cut Representation
children.top_down_role: Lifted representations of cuts generated through projection.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a polyhedron with the disjoined variable bounded by \(0\leq x_k\leq1\).
The two branch polyhedra have the recession structure represented by the homogenized branch constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lifted formulation projects to the convex hull of the two branches, and its valid inequalities involving only \(x\) are exactly the valid inequalities of that hull.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended convex-hull formulation for a binary-variable disjunction and its projected cuts.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Lift-and-Project Cuts for Mixed 0-1 Programs p. 79
2.1.1 Tightness of the Lifted Representation p. 22

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax\leq b,\ 0\leq x_k\leq1\}\), and impose the disjunction \(x_k=0\) or \(x_k=1\). Introduce \(x=x^0+x^1\), \(\lambda_0+\lambda_1=1\), and \(\lambda_0,\lambda_1\geq0\), with \(Ax^i\leq b\lambda_i\), \(x_k^0=0\), and \(x_k^1=\lambda_1\). The projection of this lifted system onto \(x\)-space is \[\operatorname{conv}\bigl((P\cap\{x:x_k=0\})\cup(P\cap\{x:x_k=1\})\bigr).\] Hence an inequality \(\alpha^Tx\leq\beta\) is valid for the displayed disjunctive hull if and only if \(\alpha^T(x^0+x^1)\leq\beta\) is valid for the lifted system. The resulting inequalities in the original variables are the lift-project cuts for this disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The homogenized two-branch formulation projects exactly to the binary disjunctive hull, and its valid inequalities in the original variables are exactly the valid inequalities of that hull.

children.title: Geometric–Lifted Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural translation between intersection and lift–project cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric–Lifted Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between forbidden-region geometry and multiplier certificates in a lifted disjunctive formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a polyhedral cone \(C\) with apex \(\bar x\) and a two-term disjunction whose excluded open region is \(S\), suppose every extreme ray of \(C\) has a well-defined first exit from \(S\). The intersection-cut inequality obtained from those exit points supports \(\operatorname{conv}(C\setminus S)\). In the homogenized two-branch formulation, nonnegative multipliers for the branch constraints produce the same supporting inequality after eliminating lifted variables. Conversely, any projected inequality admitting such branch multipliers determines supporting exit points on the rays, up to redundant rays and positive scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ray-boundary intersection data and nonnegative multipliers in the lifted disjunctive model encode the same supporting cut under regularity assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a finitely generated polyhedral cone.
The two-term disjunction induces an open convex excluded region with finite or recession-compatible ray exits.
The projected cut has a regular nonnegative branch-multiplier certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The geometric intersection cut and the projected lifted cut define the same halfspace up to positive scaling.

notation.meaning: The open region excluded by the disjunction.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 8. The Correspondence Between Lift-and-Project Cuts and Simple Disjunctive Cuts p. 97

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 8. The Correspondence Between Lift-and-Project Cuts and Simple Disjunctive Cuts p. 97

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited chapter is relevant, but the candidate's regularity assumptions are not precise enough to justify the asserted two-way correspondence. In particular, neither the class of branch-multiplier certificates nor the conditions under which a projected inequality determines ray exit points are defined. The claim that the intersection inequality supports the hull also needs explicit hypotheses. Full-text theorem-level support is required before choosing a reliable correction.

children.title: Irregular Cut Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Cases where the standard geometric correspondence fails.

knowledge_statements.title: Irregular Cut Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the standard correspondence when no regular basis-cone intersection representation exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a projected disjunctive inequality be called regular relative to an LP representation when it is obtainable, up to positive scaling, as an intersection cut from a simplicial cone associated with a feasible basis. A valid lift–project inequality is irregular relative to that representation if every nonnegative multiplier certificate producing it uses a support pattern incompatible with every such basis cone. It may remain valid and facet-defining for the disjunctive hull, but the usual basis-ray exit construction does not represent it. Thus validity of a projected disjunctive cut does not by itself guarantee a regular intersection-cut representation for a fixed formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Some valid lift–project cuts lack an intersection-cut representation from any feasible basis cone of the fixed formulation; this is representation-dependent irregularity.
assumptions_latex: A fixed LP formulation and its family of feasible basis cones are specified.
The cut is valid for the projected disjunctive hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Failure of every compatible basis-cone certificate prevents a regular intersection-cut representation without invalidating the cut.

notation.meaning: The fixed LP formulation determining the admissible basis cones.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the container, but the proposed definition of irregularity through multiplier support patterns is specialized and unsupported. A source must establish the precise formulation-relative definition and the claimed possibility of valid or facet-defining cuts without any feasible-basis intersection-cut representation.

children.title: Rank Versus One-Round Strength
children.top_down_role: Distinction between hierarchy depth and immediate relaxation improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank Versus One-Round Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates iteration depth of a closure hierarchy from objective-gap improvement in its first round.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P^{(0)}=P\) and \(P^{(t+1)}=\mathcal C(P^{(t)})\) for a cut closure \(\mathcal C\), with integer hull \(P_I\). The closure rank is \(r=\inf\{t:P^{(t)}=P_I\}\). For an objective \(c\), one-round strength may instead be measured by the reduction from \(z_0=\sup\{c^Tx:x\in P\}\) to \(z_1=\sup\{c^Tx:x\in\mathcal C(P)\}\), normalized against \(z_I=\sup\{c^Tx:x\in P_I\}\) when the denominator is nonzero. Rank is objective-independent, whereas one-round strength depends on \(c\); consequently neither quantity alone determines the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure rank counts rounds to the integer hull, while one-round strength measures objective-specific gap reduction; they are distinct comparison criteria.
assumptions_latex: The closure is iterated on the same formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Closure rank is objective-independent, while the one-round gap improvement can vary with \(c\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The distinction is plausible and the property kind fits the topic, but no source is supplied. The rank should explicitly allow infinity when the integer hull is never reached, and the advertised normalized one-round strength is not actually defined by a formula or denominator convention. A source is needed to select a standard comparison measure without inventing one.

children.title: Strong Separation Oracles
children.top_down_role: Exact separation and membership-certificate interfaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Separation Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact membership-or-separating-hyperplane interface for a closed convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a rational point \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\) and a nonempty closed convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) represented by an oracle. A strong separation oracle either returns the certificate \(y\in K\), or returns rational \((a,\beta)\) with \(a\neq0\) such that \[a^Tx\leq\beta<a^Ty\qquad\text{for every }x\in K.\] The output is an exact separating inequality: validity is required over all of \(K\), and the queried point must violate it strictly. When \(K\) is rational and well described, the encoding length of \((a,\beta)\) is included in the oracle specification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strong separation oracle either certifies exact membership or returns an exactly valid inequality strictly violated by the query point.
assumptions_latex: The oracle model specifies an exact representation of rational inputs and outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle returns membership or a strict global separator \(a^Tx\leq\beta<a^Ty\).

notation.meaning: The closed convex set being separated.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm/interface kind fits the oracle container, and the exact membership-or-strict-separator specification is coherent. However, no authoritative optimization-separation reference or locator is supplied, including for the rational output and encoding-length requirements.

children.title: Relaxed Separation Oracle Regimes
children.top_down_role: Oracle variants allowing tolerances or restricted cut families.

children.title: Weak Separation Oracles
children.top_down_role: Separation oracles providing weakened detection guarantees.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Separation Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance-based membership or separation for a bounded closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonempty bounded closed convex set \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), a query \(y\in\mathbb Q^n\), and \(\varepsilon>0\), a weak separation oracle either certifies \(\operatorname{dist}(y,K)\leq\varepsilon\), or returns a rational vector \(a\) with \(\lVert a\rVert_2=1\) satisfying \[a^Ty\geq\sup_{x\in K}a^Tx+\varepsilon.\] The two outputs need not be exclusive on a tolerance boundary. Unlike strong separation, the oracle is not required to distinguish membership from points lying within the prescribed neighborhood of \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak separation may accept points within a tolerance of the set; otherwise it returns a unit-normal separator with the prescribed margin.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is nonempty, bounded, closed, and convex.
\(\varepsilon>0\) is encoded as part of the query.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The oracle certifies \(\varepsilon\)-proximity or returns an \(\varepsilon\)-margin separator.

notation.meaning: Euclidean distance from the query point to the set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Weak separation has several inequivalent standard formulations involving inner and outer neighborhoods, approximate membership, or separator slack. The stated distance-or-margin convention therefore requires a source. Requiring an exactly rational vector with Euclidean norm one also needs justification in the specified oracle model.

children.title: Approximate Separation Oracles
children.top_down_role: Separation oracles allowing quantitative tolerances.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Separation Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive approximation to maximum normalized violation over an inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a family of valid inequalities \(a^Tx\leq b\) for \(K\), normalized by \(\lVert a\rVert_2=1\), and define \(V(y)=\sup_{(a,b)\in\mathcal F}(a^Ty-b)\). Given \(y\) and \(\varepsilon>0\), an additive approximate separation oracle returns either a certificate that \(V(y)\leq\varepsilon\), or an inequality \((\hat a,\hat b)\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \[\hat a^Ty-\hat b\geq V(y)-\varepsilon>0.\] Normalization is essential because approximation guarantees based on raw violation are otherwise changed by positive rescaling of an inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate oracle finds a valid cut whose normalized violation is within an additive tolerance of the largest available violation.
assumptions_latex: Every inequality in \(\mathcal F\) is valid for \(K\) and has a unit normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The returned cut has violation at least \(V(y)-\varepsilon\), or no family cut exceeds tolerance.

notation.meaning: The normalized family of candidate valid inequalities.
Maximum normalized family violation at the query.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The candidate defines a coherent additive approximation model after normalization, and the algorithm kind fits. It is not a source-independent definition of approximate separation, however; additive, multiplicative, and weak geometric conventions differ. A citation is required for this exact maximum-violation formulation and its certification alternative.

children.title: Restricted-Family Separation
children.top_down_role: Oracle behavior limited to a prescribed cut family.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Family Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact or approximate separation over a prescribed cut family rather than all valid inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and let \(\mathcal F\) be a specified family of inequalities valid for \(K\). On input \(y\in P\), restricted-family separation either finds \((a,b)\in\mathcal F\) with \(a^Ty>b\), or certifies that \(a^Ty\leq b\) for every \((a,b)\in\mathcal F\). This certificate establishes membership only in the family closure \[P_{\mathcal F}=P\cap\bigcap_{(a,b)\in\mathcal F}\{x:a^Tx\leq b\},\] not necessarily in \(K\). Thus failure to find a cut is globally conclusive only when \(P_{\mathcal F}=K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricted separation searches only a chosen cut family; finding no violated family cut certifies membership in that family closure, not generally the target hull.
assumptions_latex: Every member of \(\mathcal F\) is valid for \(K\).
The query point belongs to the ambient relaxation \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No violated member of \(\mathcal F\) implies \(y\in P_{\mathcal F}\), but need not imply \(y\in K\).

notation.meaning: The closure of the relaxation under that family.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The family-closure distinction is mathematically coherent and matches the terminal container, but no source supports the exact oracle interface or terminology. An authoritative cut-separation reference with a specific locator is required.

children.title: Separation Encoding-Oracle Complexity
children.top_down_role: Bit-complexity and oracle requirements underlying the equivalence.

children.title: Encoding-Length Complexity
children.top_down_role: Bit-length considerations for separation and optimization instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Encoding-Length Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity form of optimization–separation equivalence for rational, well-described polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a rational well-described polyhedron with facet-complexity bound \(\varphi\), and let rational objective \(c\) have encoding length \(L(c)\). If strong separation for \(P\) runs in time polynomial in \(n\), \(\varphi\), and the query length, then the ellipsoid reduction solves rational linear optimization over \(P\), including feasibility and unboundedness alternatives, in time polynomial in \(n\), \(\varphi\), and \(L(c)\). Conversely, a polynomial-time strong optimization oracle for the relevant rational faces yields polynomial-time strong separation. The claim is a bit-complexity result, not a strongly polynomial bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For rational well-described polyhedra, strong separation and linear optimization are polynomially equivalent in dimension and binary encoding length.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is rational and supplied with a valid facet-complexity bound.
Oracle answers have polynomially bounded rational encoding length.
Arithmetic cost is measured in the Turing bit model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation and strong linear optimization over \(P\) are polynomial-time equivalent in encoding length.

notation.meaning: Facet-complexity bound for the rational polyhedron.
Binary encoding length of the objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is correctly classified as a complexity bound, but the optimization-separation equivalence is a nontrivial theorem and has no citation. The exact well-described-polyhedron assumptions, handling of feasibility and unboundedness, output encoding bounds, and converse optimization model must be checked against an authoritative theorem statement.

children.title: Oracle-Access Complexity
children.top_down_role: Query requirements associated with separation or optimization oracles.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Access Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query bound for ellipsoid-based weak feasibility under geometric radius guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a convex body \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is contained in a known Euclidean ball of radius \(R\), and every accepted nonempty feasibility instance contains a ball of radius \(r>0\). With a separation oracle producing valid central cuts, the ellipsoid method requires \[O\!\left(n^2\log\frac{R}{r}\right)\] oracle calls to find a feasible point or reduce the enclosing ellipsoid below the promised feasible volume. Oracle-access complexity counts these calls separately from the arithmetic and encoding cost of processing each answer; polynomial query complexity therefore does not alone imply polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under inner- and outer-radius promises, ellipsoid feasibility uses order n-squared times the logarithmic radius ratio in separation-oracle calls.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) lies in a known ball of radius \(R\).
A feasible promised instance contains a Euclidean ball of radius \(r>0\).
The oracle returns valid central separating cuts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ellipsoid method uses \(O(n^2\log(R/r))\) separation-oracle calls under the stated promise.

notation.meaning: Promised inner radius of a feasible instance.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separation between oracle-query and bit complexity fits the container, but the exact \(O(n^2\log(R/r))\) bound depends on the ellipsoid update, cut depth, initialization, stopping rule, and feasibility promise. No source is supplied to fix those conventions or support the stated bound.

children.title: Strongly Polynomial Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between encoding-sensitive and strongly polynomial regimes.

assumptions_latex: The rational polytope is given by a separation oracle for \(P\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\).
Arithmetic operations and oracle calls have unit cost, while intermediate number sizes remain polynomially bounded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial optimization--separation equivalence does not, by itself, establish a strongly polynomial algorithm.

notation.meaning: Binary encoding length of the rational input and oracle data.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes encoding-polynomial equivalence from strong polynomiality in the rational oracle model.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An optimization or separation algorithm is strongly polynomial only if its number of arithmetic operations and oracle calls is bounded by a polynomial in \(n\), independently of \(L\), and every intermediate number has polynomially bounded encoding length. Standard optimization--separation reductions obtained through rational ellipsoid methods generally have running time polynomial in \(n\) and \(L\). Consequently, the existence of a polynomial-time separation oracle implies encoding-polynomial optimization, but it does not imply a strongly polynomial optimization algorithm without additional structural bounds eliminating dependence on \(L\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimization–separation equivalence is polynomial in binary input length; it is not automatically strongly polynomial because iteration counts or intermediate numbers may depend on encoding length.
knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Polynomial Boundaries

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited optimization–separation section does not specifically substantiate the stated strongly polynomial oracle model. In particular, the meaning of oracle-data encoding length and the precise permitted dependence of the operation count require an authoritative complexity reference.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polynomial-Time versus Strongly Polynomial Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding-sensitive and dimension-only running-time bounds, including the restricted-family boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For instances with $m$ constraints, $n$ variables, and largest data-coefficient size $\theta$, the stated polynomial-time regime permits a bound $T=\operatorname{poly}(m,n,\log\theta)$, whereas the stated strongly polynomial regime requires $T=\operatorname{poly}(m,n)$ with no dependence on $\theta$. If $\log\theta\leq\operatorname{poly}(m,n)$ only on a restricted family, an encoding-sensitive polynomial bound becomes polynomial in $m,n$ on that family; this restricted-family substitution does not establish a coefficient-independent bound uniformly over all instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomial time may depend polynomially on coefficient encoding length, while a strongly polynomial bound depends only on the numbers of constraints and variables. Bounding coefficient length by the dimensions on a restricted family makes the first bound dimension-polynomial only on that family and does not prove uniform strong polynomiality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{poly}}=\operatorname{poly}(m,n,\log\theta),\qquad T_{\mathrm{strong}}=\operatorname{poly}(m,n)

children.title: Separation Method Families
children.top_down_role: Exact and heuristic approaches for locating violated inequalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Heuristic and exact separation of CVRP capacity inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation of \(x(\delta(S))\ge 2\lceil d(S)/Q\rceil\) for a fractional CVRP solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact separation of the CVRP capacity inequalities is NP-hard. One heuristic forms the positive-support graph on nondepot clients and tests components having no positive-support connection to the depot. Replacing \(\lceil d(S)/Q\rceil\) by \(d(S)/Q\) yields a polynomially separable weakening. For exact separation, let \(z_i=1\) indicate \(i\in S\), impose \(z_0=0\), and use \(w_{ij}\ge z_j-z_i\) and \(w_{ij}\ge z_i-z_j\) to represent the cut. With \(\phi\in\mathbb Z_+\) and sufficiently small \(\epsilon>0\), impose \(Q^{-1}\sum_{i\ne0}d_i z_i\ge\phi+\epsilon\) and minimize \(\sum_{(i,j)\in E}x_{ij}^*w_{ij}-2(\phi+1)\). A negative optimum certifies a violated capacity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact separation of CVRP capacity cuts is NP-hard. Practical methods first test disconnected components of the fractional support graph or separate a polynomially tractable weakening. An exact mixed-integer separator selects a client set, represents its cut-set, and returns a violated capacity inequality when its objective is negative.
assumptions_latex: x^*\text{ is a nonnegative fractional CVRP solution}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{opt}<0\Longrightarrow\exists S\subseteq V\setminus\{0\}:x^*(\delta(S))<2\left\lceil\frac{d(S)}Q\right\rceil.

children.title: Structured Separation Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Graph, network, and dynamic-programming separators for structured families.

children.title: Combinatorial Separation
children.top_down_role: Graph- or network-structured searches for violated inequalities.

assumptions_latex: The inequality family is \(\mathcal F=\{a^k x\leq b_k:k\in K\}\), where \(K\) is a finite combinatorial index set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A returned index identifies a violated valid inequality; failure is exact only when the combinatorial search covers all of \(K\).

notation.meaning: Combinatorial objects indexing the inequality family.
Violation of the inequality indexed by the object.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact separation by optimizing violation over a discrete combinatorial family.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(\bar x\), compute an object \(k^*\in\arg\max_{k\in K}v(k)\) using a combinatorial algorithm specialized to \(K\). If \(v(k^*)>0\), output the valid inequality \(a^{k^*}x\leq b_{k^*}\), which separates \(\bar x\) from the relaxation defined by \(\mathcal F\). If \(v(k^*)\leq0\), certify that \(a^k\bar x\leq b_k\) for every \(k\in K\). The procedure is an exact separator precisely when the optimization over \(K\) is exact and \(K\) indexes the entire stated inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Combinatorial separation maximizes inequality violation over discrete structures and returns the structure’s cut, or certifies that no indexed inequality is violated.
knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Separation

source_witnesses.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

children.title: Dynamic-Programming Separation
children.top_down_role: State-based separation for structured cut families.

knowledge_statements.title: Dynamic-Programming Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact separation when violation maximization has a finite-stage additive dynamic-programming representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the stages be \(t=0,\ldots,T\), let \(S_t\) be the finite state set at stage \(t\), and let \(A_t\subseteq S_{t-1}\times S_t\) be the admissible transitions with contributions \(d_t(r,s)\). Initialize \(V_0(s_0)=0\) at the designated initial state \(s_0\in S_0\) and set \(V_0(s)=-\infty\) for \(s\in S_0\setminus\{s_0\}\). For \(t=1,\ldots,T\), compute \[V_t(s)=\max_{r:(r,s)\in A_t}\bigl(V_{t-1}(r)+d_t(r,s)\bigr).\] Choose \(s^*\in\arg\max_{s\in S_T}V_T(s)\) and reconstruct its index \(k^*\in K\). Under the stated path representation, \(V_T(s^*)=\max_{k\in K}v(k)\). Output the inequality indexed by \(k^*\) if \(V_T(s^*)>0\); otherwise certify that no inequality in the represented family is violated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When every indexed inequality corresponds to an admissible dynamic-programming path whose transition contributions sum to its violation, the recurrence finds a most-violated inequality and gives exact separation for that family.
assumptions_latex: The inequality family has a finite index set \(K\), and the violation of the inequality indexed by \(k\in K\) at the fixed query point is \(v(k)\).
There are stages \(t=0,\ldots,T\), finite state sets \(S_t\), an initial state \(s_0\in S_0\), and transition sets \(A_t\subseteq S_{t-1}\times S_t\).
Every \(k\in K\) is represented by an admissible path from \(s_0\) to \(S_T\), every such path represents an index in \(K\), and its transition contributions sum to \(v(k)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The terminal optimum equals \(\max_{k\in K}v(k)\), so the procedure is an exact separator for the represented family.

notation.meaning: Finite set indexing the represented inequality family.
Finite state set at stage t.
Admissible transitions from stage t-1 to stage t.
Violation contribution of transition (r,s) at stage t.
Best accumulated violation of a path reaching state s at stage t.
Inequality index reconstructed from an optimal terminal path.

children.title: Graph-Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cut families whose separation reduces to graph problems.

assumptions_latex: The inequality indices are feasible substructures \(H\) of a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\).
For the query point \(\bar x\), violation is equivalent to a graph objective crossing a known threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Solving the corresponding graph optimization problem exactly gives an exact separator for the graph-indexed family.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph reductions in which a most-violated inequality is a graph optimization problem.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Some graph theory p. 8
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each \(H\in\mathcal H(G)\) indexes a valid inequality and there is a threshold \(\tau\) such that this inequality is violated by \(\bar x\) exactly when \(w_{\bar x}(H)<\tau\). Then separation is represented by the graph problem \[H^*\in\arg\min_{H\in\mathcal H(G)}w_{\bar x}(H).\] If \(w_{\bar x}(H^*)<\tau\), output the inequality indexed by \(H^*\); otherwise no member of the graph-indexed family is violated. Polynomial-time exact separation follows whenever this graph problem is polynomially solvable and its weights have polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When violations correspond to low-weight graph structures, an exact graph optimizer either identifies a violated cut or certifies the whole indexed family.
knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Separation Regimes

children.title: Network-Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cut families whose separation exploits network structure.

assumptions_latex: The cut family is indexed by feasible objects in a directed or undirected network \(D=(V,A)\).
Query-dependent arc weights have polynomial encoding length.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A polynomial-time exact network optimizer yields polynomial-time exact separation for the represented inequality family.

notation.meaning: Query-dependent cost of an indexing object.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separation reductions to minimum cut, shortest path, flow, or related network optimization.

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Some graph theory p. 8
source_refs.source_title: Theory of Linear and Integer Programming

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct from \(\bar x\) a network objective \(c_{\bar x}\) and solve \[N^*\in\arg\min_{N\in\mathcal N(D)}c_{\bar x}(N).\] Assume that the inequality indexed by \(N\) is violated exactly when \(c_{\bar x}(N)<\tau\), for a specified threshold \(\tau\). If \(c_{\bar x}(N^*)<\tau\), return that inequality; otherwise certify absence of a violation in the represented family. This is an exact polynomial-time separator when the construction is polynomial and the relevant minimum-cut, shortest-path, flow, or circulation problem is solved exactly in polynomial time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Network separation translates maximum violation into an exact minimum-cut, path, flow, or circulation computation with a specified violation threshold.

children.title: Optimization-Based Separation
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary linear, integer, or conic models used to search a cut family.

assumptions_latex: The candidate family is parameterized by \(y\in Y\), with every inequality \(a(y)x\leq b(y)\) valid for the target set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimizer with positive objective supplies a separating inequality; a nonpositive exact optimum certifies familywise feasibility.

notation.meaning: Feasible parameter set of the auxiliary separation model.
Violation objective at the query point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Auxiliary linear, integer, or conic optimization over parameters of a valid-inequality family.

source_refs.locator: 6.5 Optimization and Separation p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Form the auxiliary optimization problem \[\phi^*=\max_{y\in Y}\{a(y)\bar x-b(y)\}.\] Solve it exactly using the applicable linear, integer, or conic optimization method. If an optimizer \(y^*\) satisfies \(\phi(y^*)>0\), output \(a(y^*)x\leq b(y^*)\), which is valid for the target set and violated by \(\bar x\). If \(\phi^*\leq0\), certify that \(a(y)\bar x\leq b(y)\) for every \(y\in Y\). When the auxiliary problem is solved only locally or approximately, the final alternative is not an exact separation certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimization-based separation maximizes violation in an auxiliary model and converts a positive optimizer into a valid cut.
knowledge_statements.title: Optimization-Based Separation
